 Supreme Court Supreme Court rejects Trump over academic funding cuts related to DEI
 University of California researchers say the abrupt funding cuts violated their First Amendment rights. Listen to this article with a free profile 00:00 00:00 President Donald Trump on the South Lawn of the White House last week. Aaron Schwartz / Sipa / Bloomberg via Getty Share Add NBC News to Google Nov. 16, 2026, 9:52 AM EST By Lawrence Hurley WASHINGTON — The Supreme Court on Monday rejected President Donald Trump’s move to abruptly cancel academic funding for researchers in California because his administration deemed the projects to be inconsistent with policies such as his opposition to DEI initiatives.
 The court left in place lower court rulings that said the government violated the free speech rights under the Constitution’s 1st Amendment by terminating grants issued to University of California researchers.
 Upon taking office in January 2025, Trump issued several executive orders telling agencies to ensure funding was consistent with his views opposing diversity, equity and inclusion programs, as well as such issues as climate change and transgender rights.

 Slide 1 of 1 At issue in the Supreme Court appeal were grants issued by the National Science Foundation and the National Endowment for the Humanities.
 In total, the federal government tried to end $324 million in funding to University of California institutions as part of a nationwide purge, although some funding has since resumed.

 Slide 1 of 1 Affected researchers sued, saying that the decisions discriminated against them based on their views. They alleged that the grants were cut based on keyword searches looking for words or phrases disfavored by the administration, such as “diversity” or “climate change.”
 Both a federal judge and the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals agreed with the plaintiffs that the terminations violated free speech rights. 
 But in a separate part of the case not at issue in the Supreme Court, the appeals court ruled that the plaintiffs would have to file a separate lawsuit in the Court of Federal Claims if they wanted to recoup lost funding.
